en: Raised reflective road markers that help show where lanes and edges are, especially at night.
Small rectangular signs placed under a main road sign that add details such as times or exceptions.
Side-to-side swinging of a trailer or caravan while being towed, which can become dangerous.
A sudden change of direction to avoid something, such as a pothole or slippery patch.
Suddenly changing direction, often to avoid something in the road.
Moves out to the right before turning left—common for long vehicles that need more space.
The red lights at the rear of a vehicle that show its position to drivers behind.
Paying UK vehicle tax (VED) so the vehicle can be used on public roads.
Something briefly blocking or slowing traffic, such as a stopped vehicle.
A speed limit that applies only for a limited time, often near roadworks.
A motorway with three lanes in each direction of travel.
Lenses that are darkened or coloured, reducing how much light reaches your eyes.
A metric unit of weight used on UK restriction signs for heavy vehicles.
The ball-shaped coupling on a tow bar that the trailer hitch locks onto.
The metal bar fitted to a vehicle for attaching and towing a trailer or caravan.
A caravan being pulled behind another vehicle on the road.
Pulling a trailer attached behind your vehicle.
Pulling a trailer, caravan, or another vehicle behind your car using a tow bar or hitch.
A slow agricultural vehicle often seen on country roads; overtaking needs clear space and time.
An official authorised to manage traffic on motorways and some major roads.
Specialist road staff who manage incidents and traffic on motorways and major A-roads.
Road features such as humps or narrowings designed to keep vehicle speeds lower.
An unpowered wheeled unit designed to be towed behind a vehicle to carry loads.
Electric passenger vehicles that run on rails set into the road surface.
Lines painted across the road (often yellow) to alert you as you approach a hazard.
Yellow lines painted across the road (from side to side), not along it.
How deep the grooves in a tyre are; worn-down tread reduces grip, especially in wet weather.
A red-bordered triangle road sign that warns of a hazard ahead.
A road passage that goes under ground or through a hill.
A rule of thumb: stay at least two seconds behind the vehicle ahead in good, dry conditions.
In good, dry conditions, keep at least a two-second gap behind the vehicle ahead.
A road where traffic travels in both directions.
Roads where traffic travels in both directions.
How well the tyres hold the road surface for steering and braking.
How much air is in each tyre; incorrect pressure affects handling, braking, and tyre wear.
How much air is in each tyre; incorrect pressure affects handling, braking, and tyre wear.
How the tyre rubber wears down; uneven wear can signal a fault.
Left alone with no one in or watching the vehicle.
A trailer without its own brakes; coupling safety devices are especially important.
Not awake and not responding; may need emergency help.
Tyres with too little air pressure, which can worsen handling and wear.
A road that is bumpy or irregular rather than smooth.
A road with no street lighting at night.
A junction where roads meet with no give-way or stop signs or road markings.
A section of road going up a slope.
An urban road where stopping is restricted during posted times, except briefly for passengers.
Air and noise pollution in towns and cities, often from traffic.
Temporary speed limits shown on overhead signs that change with traffic conditions.
Who legally owns the vehicle; changes of ownership must be recorded with the DVLA.
Another name for the V5C registration document showing vehicle and keeper details.
The V5C paper that records the vehicle’s details and its registered keeper.
The official number plate details that identify a vehicle.
The UK road tax (VED) you must pay to use a vehicle on public roads.
The soft or grassy edge beside the road, not meant for normal driving.
UK phrase meaning you can see only a short distance, often under about 100 metres.
More at risk of injury in a collision because of little physical protection (e.g. bikes, motorcycles, pedestrians).
A parking or traffic warden who enforces parking rules.
A red reflective triangle placed on the road to warn others of a broken-down vehicle.
Water collecting in low spots on the road after rain.
When drive wheels spin too fast on a slippery surface and lose grip.
A road with many bends, where overtaking is often difficult and slow traffic can build up.
The upright frames at the edges of the windscreen that can block part of your view.
A cone-shaped cloth tube that shows wind direction and strength; used as a road-sign symbol.
Yellow road markings at the kerb that restrict waiting or parking.
A pedestrian crossing with black-and-white stripes where drivers must give way to people waiting to cross.
A pedestrian crossing with black-and-white stripes where drivers must give way to people waiting to cross.
Yellow zig-zag lines near crossings or schools where you must not park or stop and block the view.
Zigzag road markings near crossings; parking and waiting there is restricted.
